claims.text: Resistance of high-entropy alloys to simultaneous wear and corrosion is governed by a continuously regenerating, self-healing, multi-component oxide film.
The regenerating oxide film protects against mechanical degradation.
The regenerating oxide film protects against chemical degradation.
The proposed initial material is a homogenized high-entropy alloy with a uniform microstructure.
A uniform microstructure predisposes the alloy to rapid oxide formation.
The proposed test simultaneously applies cyclic sliding or abrasion and corrosive attack in an oxygenated saline or chloride-rich environment.
Intermittent wear-induced surface damage permits oxide-film reformation under oxygenated conditions.
High configurational entropy promotes rapid formation and regeneration of a robust oxide layer during wear-induced damage.
The regenerated oxide layer limits mechanical material loss.
The regenerated oxide layer limits electrochemical corrosion.
Under simultaneous wear and corrosion, the oxide-optimized alloy should have lower wear-volume loss than a mechanically matched baseline lacking self-healing oxide capability.
Under simultaneous wear and corrosion, the oxide-optimized alloy should have a lower corrosion rate than the baseline.
The predicted improvement should occur under oxygen-rich, moderate-load conditions.
The protective effect should diminish in oxygen-deprived environments.
The protective effect may fail under extreme mechanical damage when oxide regeneration cannot keep pace with oxide removal.
The magnitude of improvement depends on the testing conditions and alloy composition.
Failure to observe significantly reduced wear and corrosion losses in the oxide-optimized alloy under oxygen-rich conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to observe a robust, regenerating oxide film would falsify the hypothesis.
